'''Daniel Steven Nagin''' (born November 29, 1948)<ref name=lc>{{Cite web |url=http://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/n78022019.html |title=Nagin, Daniel |website=Library of Congress}}</ref> is an American criminologist, [[statistician]], and the Teresa and H. John Heinz III University Professor of Public Policy and Statistics at [[Carnegie Mellon University]]'s [[Heinz College]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://sites.nationalacademies.org/DBASSE/CLAJ/DBASSE_082260 | title=Daniel S. Nagin | work=Committee on Law and Justice | accessdate=23 January 2016 | archive-date=27 August 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160827225707/http://sites.nationalacademies.org/DBASSE/CLAJ/DBASSE_082260 | url-status=dead }}</ref> He was elected a Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2025.<ref>https://www.nasonline.org/news/2025-nas-election/</ref>
==Education==
Nagin received his B.S. in Administrative and Managerial Sciences and M.S. in Industrial Administration from [[Carnegie Mellon University]] in 1971, and his Ph.D. from what is now the university's Heinz College in 1976.<ref name=cmu>{{cite web | url=http://www.heinz.cmu.edu/faculty-and-research/faculty-profiles/faculty-details/index.aspx?faculty_id=69 | title=Daniel Nagin | work=Carnegie Mellon University | accessdate=23 January 2016 | archive-date=30 January 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160130060841/http://www.heinz.cmu.edu/faculty-and-research/faculty-profiles/faculty-details/index.aspx?faculty_id=69 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
Nagin served as Deputy Secretary for Fiscal Policy and Analysis in the [[Pennsylvania Department of Revenue]] from 1981 to 1986.<ref name=cmu/> He joined Carnegie Mellon University in 1986 as an associate professor of management in the School of Urban and Public Affairs. In 1990, he became professor of management in Heinz College, a position he retained until 1998.<ref name="cv">{{cite web | url=http://www.heinz.cmu.edu/faculty/69cv.pdf | title=Daniel S. Nagin CV | accessdate=23 January 2016 | archive-date=16 September 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150916170904/http://www.heinz.cmu.edu/faculty/69cv.pdf | url-status=dead }}</ref> He was also the research program area director of Carnegie Mellon University's National Consortium on Violence Research from 1997 to 2001.<ref name=cv/> In 2006, he became the Associate Dean of Faculty at Heinz College, and in 2008, he became the Teresa and H. John Heinz III University Professor of Public Policy and Statistics, positions he still held as of December 2019.<ref name=cv/>

==Research==
Nagin is known for researching the deterrence effect of criminal punishments and he chaired the [[National Research Council (United States)|National Research Council]]’s Committee on Deterrence and the Death Penalty.<ref name=cmu/> In 2012, this committee released a report concluding that existing research on the deterrent effect of [[capital punishment]] is inconclusive.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/wonk/wp/2014/04/30/theres-still-no-evidence-that-executions-deter-criminals/ | title=There's still no evidence that executions deter criminals | newspaper=Washington Post | date=30 April 2013 | accessdate=23 January 2016 | author=Ehrenfreund, Max}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://content.usatoday.com/communities/sciencefair/post/2012/04/nrc-death-penalty-effect-research-fundamentally-flawed/1 | title=NRC: Death penalty effect research "fundamentally flawed" | work=USA Today | date=18 April 2012 | accessdate=3 October 2016 | author=Vergano, Dan}}</ref> He has also researched the use of statistical methods for analyzing longitudinal data, as well as changes in criminal behavior over the human lifetime.<ref name=cmu/>

==Honors and awards==
Nagin, along with [[Joan Petersilia]], received the [[Stockholm Prize in Criminology]] in 2014. He received the Edwin H. Sutherland Award from the [[American Society of Criminology]] in 2006.<ref name=press/> In 2017, he received the NAS Award for Scientific Reviewing from the [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://annualreviewsnews.org/2017/01/25/nas-award-winner-17/ |title=Congratulations to Daniel S. Nagin, winner of the 2017 NAS Award for Scientific Reviewing |date=2017-01-25 |website=Annual Reviews News |language=en-US |access-date=2018-01-24}}</ref> He is also a fellow of the American Society of Criminology, the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and the [[American Academy of Political and Social Science]].<ref name=cmu/>
